item.title: Are You Thinking About Thinking Too Much?
item.description:
Cognition

Are You Thinking About Thinking Too Much?

It's time to get out of your head and into your senses.

Posted August 26, 2026

Key points
  • While some people are aware of their thoughts always running, they sruggle to identify their emotions.
  • Common causes include childhood trauma, hypervigilance, generalized anxiety, depression, and self-criticism.
  • The way out of overanalyzing is to slow down and practice becoming more aware of sensory experiences.
"The Thinker"
Source: Rodin Museum Image / Pixabay

Maybe your head is always running, a nonstop stream of thoughts, double- and triple-analyzing every little thing. Or when someone asks how you feel, your first response is to think about what might really be behind their question, or to think about thinking about how you’re feeling, but you can never cut through the layers of thought and get down to that emotional bottom floor. If you’re looking for a break from this constant mental chatter, or if you sense that your thinking is like a blanket smothering your emotions, maybe it’s time to begin rewiring your brain.

But first, let’s look at some common causes:

Childhood trauma and numbing

I’ve met hundreds of clients who, unfortunately, experienced childhood trauma and say they feel nothing. They are aware of their thoughts but are numb from the neck down. This absolutely makes sense; it is their brain’s protective mechanism to keep those strong traumatic experiences at bay. They often dissociate in stressful situations.

Hypervigilance

In contrast to numbness, some people exposed to traumatic situations become hypervigilant: always looking around corners, hypersensitive to what others are doing, feeling, and wanting, and constantly looking into the future and to what-ifs. Because they are understandably so externally focused, their internal, emotional life never fully develops.

Generalized anxiety

Those who are hypervigilant as children remain anxious as adults. But even apart from any trauma, if you grow up in a family with anxious parents, you, too, can develop anxiety. One effect of anxiety that I’ve observed over the years is that those prone to anxiety often struggle to identify other emotions—anxiety is their primary emotion, and other emotions are buried beneath it.

Depression

A depressed mind is like a heavy weight suppressing thoughts, emotions, and behaviors, but a mind that can ruminate endlessly circles the same mental drain, blocking out other thoughts and emotions.

Self-criticism and perfectionism

If you tend to be self-critical and/or perfectionistic, and you fear making a mistake, it makes sense that you will overthink whatever you do or decide.

To calm your overthinking brain, do what you’re not doing: rewire it by focusing on the present rather than the past or the future, and on your emotions rather than your thoughts. Here are four suggestions:

1. Get into your senses.

The smells of dinner cooking. The bright blue sky. The feeling of your muscles working at the gym, the sound of birds outside, or the slicing of a tomato while you are cooking.

Being aware of your senses helps ground you. For example, one technique to help children who are behaviorally out of control or emotionally overwhelmed is to have them do exactly that—pick out three blue objects in the room, identify four different sounds, and notice two different odors. It works by shifting them from their anxious brains to their rational, mindful brain.

Likely, your five senses are underdeveloped for good reasons. Developing your senses starts with awareness. This means avoiding the tendency to think you need to pay attention to your senses and then to think your way through it, and instead simply noting what you experience—the odor, the birds, the muscles. You can also enhance your sensations by slowing down—slowly cutting that tomato, slowly lifting that weight at the gym.

2. Shift your focus.

If increasing your sensory awareness means noticing when those experiences sneak up on you, you can also be more proactive by practicing shifting your focus. There’s a lot of talk these days about mindfulness, but if you’re an overthinker, that can just mean thinking about how to do mindfulness right.

Instead, rewire your brain by deliberately doing something that takes you out of your thinking mode and forces you to concentrate. Usually, learning something new is best: a language, drawing, or playing an instrument. These experiences not only help you learn new skills but also rewire your brain to shift into that mindful mode.

3. Follow your passions.

If reconnecting with your senses is important for expanding your experience, learning to use your emotions, rather than your thoughts, is the other half of the puzzle. This means cultivating even the slightest wisp of emotion. Going out for lunch instead of sitting at your desk. Going salsa dancing even though it’s a Tuesday. Calling up your high school friend whom you haven’t talked to in years because you felt the urge to do so.

It is not about the lunch, the dancing, or the friend, but about rewiring your brain to use emotions as information about what you need and desire.

4. Consider medication.

I know your thinking brain is worried and analyzing possible side effects, about becoming dependent on medication or needing to stay on it forever. But medication can help break the overthinking cycle, slow your anxious brain, and make it easier to try the suggestions above. Consider a consultation and go in with questions about all your reservations.

Overthinking is a protective byproduct of past experiences, but it doesn’t have to be the only way your brain operates. Maybe it’s time to slow it down.
